content.text: An ad hoc command is one task, once. A playbook is a saved, shareable, version-controllable YAML file that can define many tasks, across many plays, applied to many different hosts — everything ad hoc commands can't do.
Only SPACE characters — tabs are never allowed. Items at the same level need identical indentation; children must be indented further than their parent
A playbook begins with three dashes (---); an end marker (...) is legal but almost always omitted
Each item starts with a dash and a space (- item)

A play has three commonly-used top-level keys: name (an optional label — always use it, especially once a playbook has multiple plays), hosts (which inventory hosts/groups this play targets), and tasks (the ordered list of things to do).

⚠ WARNING A missing space after a colon is one of the most common YAML syntax errors — name:hosts (no space) is invalid YAML and will fail with a cryptic 'mapping values are not allowed in this context' error, not an obviously helpful one.

Run the exact same playbook again and the task now reports ok instead of changed, with changed=0 in the recap — idempotence, visible directly in the output. Gathering Facts is a special automatic task (covered fully in Section 2.5) that runs before your first task in almost every play, whether you asked for it or not.
Adds connection details to managed hosts
Adds connection plug-in internals — the remote user, scripts executed
Parse the playbook for YAML/Ansible syntax errors WITHOUT running it
Dry run — reports what WOULD change, makes no actual changes

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT --syntax-check and -C (check mode) are two DIFFERENT safety nets and are often tested as a pair: syntax-check only catches YAML/structural errors (a missing colon, bad indentation) — it does NOT verify that tasks will actually succeed. -C mode actually connects to managed hosts and evaluates what each task WOULD do, without changing anything — which catches a much broader class of problems, but still isn't a full guarantee (a task that depends on another task's side effect can behave differently in a real run).

✗ COMMON MISTAKE Treating a clean --syntax-check as proof the playbook will work. It only proves the YAML parses — a task referencing a module that doesn't exist, or a host that isn't reachable, passes syntax-check without issue and only fails at actual run time (or shows up correctly under -C).

sections.title: 2. Multiple Plays, Per-Play Privilege, and YAML Variations

content.text: A single playbook can contain multiple plays, each targeting different hosts — useful for orchestrating a deployment where different tiers need different tasks in sequence.
Each play runs completely — against all of its targeted hosts — before the next play begins.
Overrides the default connection user for just this play
Overrides privilege escalation for just this play
Overrides HOW to escalate for just this play
Overrides WHICH user to become for just this play

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS This is exactly the same become/remote_user logic from Part 1's ansible.cfg — playbooks just let you override it per play instead of globally, for the (common) case where one play needs different privileges than another in the same file.
The -s option is worth using constantly — it prints a ready-to-copy YAML task skeleton for the module, showing every available option, instead of the full prose documentation.
YAML syntax variations you'll see in the wild
Use for content like config file blocks
Avoid — harder to read (except for role parameters, covered later)
Avoid — harder to read than the dash-list form
Recognize it in older playbooks; don't write new tasks this way

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT Know that the key=value shorthand syntax for tasks still exists and still works — you will see it in older playbooks and documentation examples — but the modern, expected style is the nested YAML dictionary form used throughout this guide. The exam expects you to read both but write the modern form.
Spaces, dots, dashes, or start with a number
Three scope levels — narrower always wins

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT Memorize the direction, not just the names: inventory-defined variables are overridden by playbook-defined variables, which are overridden by command-line extra variables (-e). A narrower, more specific scope always beats a wider one — this exact precedence question shows up directly on both RHCSA and RHCE-adjacent material.
Defining and using variables in a playbook

⚠ WARNING When a value starts WITH a variable reference, quotes are mandatory: name: "{{ user }}" — without them, Ansible can misparse {{ as the start of a YAML dictionary and fail with a confusing error. A variable used in the MIDDLE of a string (Creates the user {{ user }}) does not need quotes.
For a large or shared set of variables, vars_files pulls them from an external YAML file instead of inlining them:
Host and group variables — the preferred pattern

Defining ansible_user=joe directly in the inventory file works, but is the OLD, discouraged approach — it mixes host data and variable data in one file. The preferred pattern is two sibling directories next to the inventory:
│ ├── datacenters # applies to the whole datacenters group
A file's name must exactly match the group or host it applies to; its content is plain YAML key-value pairs, same as a vars: block.

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT Host variables (host_vars) take precedence over group variables (group_vars), which are overridden by variables defined directly in the playbook. This is the SAME narrower-wins principle as the three scope levels, just applied one level more granularly within the 'host/inventory' scope.
register captures a task's result into a variable for later use — commonly paired with the debug module to inspect it:

Playbooks often need real secrets — API keys, database passwords. Ansible Vault encrypts any structured data file (AES256) so secrets can live safely alongside the rest of a version-controlled project.
Create a brand-new encrypted file (prompts for a password, opens $EDITOR)
Read an encrypted file's contents WITHOUT decrypting it to disk
Decrypt to a temp file, let you edit, re-encrypt on save
Encrypt one or more existing plaintext files
Permanently decrypt a file back to plaintext

✗ COMMON MISTAKE Using edit just to look at a file's contents. edit always rewrites the file on save (even if nothing meaningfully changed), which creates noisy diffs in version control. Use view for read-only inspection, every time.
Running a playbook that touches Vault-encrypted files
Prompt interactively for the password (the modern, Ansible 2.4+ syntax)
Older interactive-prompt syntax; still works if all encrypted files share one password
Read the password from a plaintext file (protect that file's permissions carefully)

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT Multiple different vault passwords can be used in one playbook run with repeated --vault-id id@prompt options. Without a password provided at all, ansible-playbook fails immediately with 'A vault password must be specified' — it never silently skips the encrypted content.

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS The recommended real-world pattern: keep NON-sensitive variables in a plain group_vars/host_vars file, and put ONLY the sensitive ones in a separate file that gets encrypted with Vault (e.g. vars/secret.yml alongside vars/main.yml). This keeps most of your project readable and diff-friendly in version control, while still protecting the parts that actually matter.

Facts are variables Ansible automatically discovers ABOUT each managed host — hostname, kernel version, IP addresses, CPU count, free memory, and much more — collected before your first task runs, via the automatic Gathering Facts step (which runs the setup module behind the scenes).
Dictionary-style facts can also be written with dot notation: ansible_facts['default_ipv4']['address'] and ansible_facts.default_ipv4.address are equivalent.

🔎 REAL-WORLD EXTENSION Older playbooks (and plenty of documentation) use facts 'injected as variables' directly — ansible_hostname instead of ansible_facts['hostname']. Both still work, but ansible_facts['name'] is the current recommended form; recognize the old style when you see it.
- name: This play gathers no facts automatically

Disabling it speeds up plays that never reference facts, or is necessary when a managed host genuinely can't run the setup module yet (e.g. before a prerequisite is installed). Facts can still be gathered manually inside such a play with an explicit setup: task.

Administrators can define their own custom facts on a managed host (as static INI/JSON files, or executable scripts producing JSON) placed under a facts.d directory — the setup module automatically folds these into the standard fact set, giving hosts a way to expose arbitrary local information to Ansible.
Every managed host's variables — lets one host's tasks reference ANOTHER host's variables/facts
The list of groups the CURRENT host belongs to
Every group AND host defined in the whole inventory
The current host's name exactly as written in the inventory (which may differ from its real hostname fact)

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT hostvars is what makes cross-host configuration possible — e.g. a web server's config file template referencing the database server's IP address via hostvars['db1.example.com']['ansible_default_ipv4']['address']. This pattern is common in real playbooks and worth recognizing even before Part 4 covers templates in depth.

labs.title: Lab: A Real Playbook with Variables, Facts, and a Secret

content.text: Write a multi-play, variable-driven playbook that uses group_vars, a Vault-protected secret, a registered variable, and a fact-based debug message.

Provision two web servers and one database server. The web servers need a package installed (name varies by group_vars), and a debug message showing each host's detected IP address. The database server needs a sensitive root password set from an encrypted variable file.
A control node with a project directory ~/ansible-lab2, an inventory with [webservers] (web1, web2) and [dbservers] (db1)
2. Create a Vault-encrypted file vars/db_secret.yml containing db_root_password: SomeSecretValue

3. Write a playbook with two plays: one for webservers (install {{ package }}, register the result, debug-print each host's ansible_facts['default_ipv4']['address']), one for dbservers (loads vars/db_secret.yml via vars_files, and uses a debug task to confirm the variable loaded — do NOT print the actual secret value)
4. Run --syntax-check, then a dry run (-C) with the vault password supplied, then a real run

Print db_root_password itself only if you want it showing up in your terminal history and any logs — a debug task confirming a variable is 'defined' (using the Jinja2 test {{ db_root_password is defined }}) proves it loaded without echoing the secret.

Before checking the solution: does your playbook run cleanly with --syntax-check but then fail at actual run time with 'a vault password must be specified'? That's expected and correct — syntax-check never touches Vault-encrypted content.
- name: Confirm secret loaded without printing it
msg: "db_root_password is defined: {{ db_root_password is defined }}"
group_vars/webservers means the package name is resolved automatically for any host in that group — no per-host repetition needed.
vars_files inside the second play scopes the encrypted secret to ONLY that play, rather than loading it globally where the web server play could accidentally reference it too.
The is defined Jinja2 test confirms the variable exists without ever putting its actual value into terminal output or logs — good practice for anything Vault-protected.
register + a later debug task is the standard way to inspect what a task actually did, exactly as covered in Section 2.3.

The webservers play's debug output should show a real IP address per host, sourced from gathered facts, not something you typed. Running the whole playbook a second time should show ok (not changed) for the package install task, proving idempotence held even with variables in play.

Splitting non-sensitive config (group_vars) from sensitive config (a Vault-encrypted vars file loaded via vars_files, scoped to only the play that needs it) is exactly the recommended production pattern from Section 2.4 — this lab is that pattern, not a simplified version of it.
Q1. What character is NEVER allowed for indentation in a YAML playbook?
Answer: The tab character — only spaces are allowed.
Q2. What's the practical difference between --syntax-check and -C (dry run)?
Answer: --syntax-check only validates YAML/structural syntax without connecting to any host; -C actually connects to managed hosts and reports what WOULD change, without making real changes.
Q3. List the three variable scope levels from highest to lowest precedence.
Answer: Global (command-line -e / ansible.cfg) → Play (vars:/vars_files: in the playbook) → Host/inventory (inventory, group_vars/host_vars, facts, registered variables).
Q4. When must a variable reference be wrapped in quotes in a task?
Answer: When the variable reference STARTS the value, e.g. name: "{{ user }}" — without quotes, Ansible can misinterpret {{ as starting a YAML dictionary.
Q5. What are the two preferred directories for defining host and group variables, replacing the old inline inventory syntax?
Answer: group_vars/ and host_vars/, as sibling directories next to the inventory file.
Q6. What's the difference between ansible-vault edit and ansible-vault view?
Answer: edit decrypts to a temp file, lets you change it, and re-encrypts on save (always rewrites the file); view only displays contents without ever writing a decrypted copy or modifying the file.
Q7. What happens if you run ansible-playbook against a playbook that references a Vault-encrypted file, without providing any vault password option?
Answer: It fails immediately with an error stating a vault password must be specified — it never silently skips or ignores the encrypted content.
Q8. What does register do in a task, and what module is it typically paired with to inspect the result?
Answer: It captures the task's result into a named variable; typically paired with the debug module to print that variable's value.
Q9. What does the magic variable hostvars let you do that facts alone can't?
Answer: Access ANOTHER managed host's variables/facts from within a task running against a different host — enabling cross-host configuration (e.g. a web server referencing the database server's IP).
Q10. How do you disable automatic fact gathering for a play, and can facts still be gathered manually afterward?
Answer: Set gather_facts: no at the play level; facts can still be gathered manually at any point with an explicit task using the setup module.
RH294 — RED HAT SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION III: LINUX AUTOMATION

This Part covers RH294 Chapter 5 in full — loops, conditionals, handlers, and controlling exactly what counts as failure or change. This is the chapter that turns a playbook from a straight-line script into something that actually reasons about the state of each host it touches.

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS Real infrastructure is never uniform — some hosts need five users, some need two; some tasks should only run on RedHat, others only when a previous step actually changed something. Everything in this Part exists to handle that variation without writing a separate playbook for every possible combination.
